headline: Approved new equity standards for marijuana retail businesses and raised the pension cost-of-living base to $15,000.
summary: Residents raised concerns about the 10 Hudson Road development, including blasting and loss of mature trees. Councilors also heard an update on the city's electricity aggregation program and approved six utility petitions and two grants. A motion to reconsider the pension increase vote failed, with 8 opposed and none in favor.

Councilors Present: Council President, Councilor Tony Gross; Council Vice President, Councilor Sean

Francesco Margiotta; Councilor Dylan Benson; Councilor Marjorie Grace
Absent: Councilor Jason Grow

This meeting was conducted with the City Council in person
and the public participating in person and remotely via Zoom.
Meeting called to order at 6:30 p.m.
Councilor Gross stated the following:
“This public meeting of the City Council is recorded on zoom with a link that is posted on the agenda. If you
are calling in on a phone, you can press Star 9 to request to speak. If you are watching on a computer or device,
there is a “raised hand” button that you can tap or press to request to speak. Please use either of these options
during oral communications and public hearings to be recognized to speak.
If technical difficulties arise and the Zoom link is interrupted during an in-person hybrid meeting of the City
Council and a quorum is present, the meeting may continue after efforts have been made to reestablish the link.
The minutes shall note the interruption.
It is the finding of the City of Gloucester that no individual should be denied equal treatment or opportunity
because of their age, ancestry, color, disability, including intellectual and developmental mental disability,
family status, immigration status, gender identity or expression, military status, marital status, national origin,
race, religion, sex or sexual orientation.”
FLAG SALUTE AND MOMENT OF SILENCE: Councilor Page led the flag salute.
ORAL COMMUNICATIONS: Emily Presti-Giovanni, 11 Nally Avenue, stated her and her neighborhoods
concerns regarding the development at the 10 Hudson Road property. These included concerns regarding blasting,
fire suppression, snow removal, and loss of mature trees. 
Kathy Interrante, 9 Nally Avenue, stated her concerns regarding the development of 10 Hudson Road. She
stated that blasting may damage surrounding properties. 
Susan Altenburger, 66 Atlantic Street, stated her concerns regarding the state of the fishing industry.

PRESENTATIONS/COMMENDATIONS: Update on the City of Gloucester Community Electricity
Aggregation Program by Rachel Ferdinand, Program Manager and Stefano Loretto, Business Development
Director of Good Energy, LP.
Planning Director, Gregg Cademartori stated that this program was an aggregate program that allowed for the
reduction of electrical bills. He stated that the program had been running since 2018.
Stefano Loretto, Business Development Director of Good Energy, LP shared his screen.
Stefano Loretto stated the above.

Councilor Page asked if current members of the aggregate program would be automatically enrolled in the
updated program. Stefano Loretto stated they would.
Councilor Page stated that if aggregate program members wanted the cheapest option, then they needed to change
from the default option to the basic option, and that National Grid offered a battery program for those with heat
pumps. 
Councilor Benson asked what the average savings were for those in the aggregate program per year. Stefano
Loretto stated that the average savings was between $1,700 and $2,000 per residential account.
Councilor Nolan asked if there were any work done to assist residents who had older homes with electric heat.
Stefano Loretto stated that it depended on National Grid regulations and State mandates, but smart meters should
help with those issues. 
Councilor Gross asked if those in budgeted billing would be affected. Stefano Loretto stated that they would
not. 
Councilor Kimberley asked if the program went door-to-door. Stefano Loretto stated that it did not.
Councilor Grace asked if a resident would be able to tell on their National Grid bill that they were already in the
program. Stefano Loretto stated that it would be under the delivery and supply charges section of the bill.
Councilor Benson asked how much the City had reduced its carbon footprint with the program. Stefano Loretto
stated that 63 million pounds of CO2 had been displaced.
Councilor Gross asked if all of this information was available to City residents on the City website. Gregg
Cademartori stated it was.

Chapter 28 MARIJUANA RETAIL ESTABLISHMENTS
ADD ARTICLE II. – EQUITY STANDARDS FOR PROMOTING AND ENCOURAGING FULL 
PARTICIPATION IN THE REGULATED MARIJUANA INDUSTRY
Sec. 28-3. Legislative Authority
This ordinance is authorized pursuant to St. 2022, c. 180, an act relative to equity in the cannabis industry, 
M.G.L. c. 94G and M.G.L. c. 94I, 935 CMR §§ 500.000, and §§ 501.000. 
Sec. 28-4. Purpose
The intent of this ordinance is to comply with M.G.L. c. 94G § 4(a) and 935 CMR 500.181 and 501.181.
Sec. 28-5. Applicability
This ordinance shall apply to all individuals and entities seeking to locate a marijuana establishment or medical 
marijuana treatment center within the City. No individual or entity shall operate a marijuana establishment or a 
medical marijuana treatment center unless duly licensed to do so by the Cannabis Control Commission. Nothing
in this section shall be construed to supersede federal and state laws governing the sale and distribution of 
marijuana.
Sec. 28-6. Definitions
The definitions set forth in M.G.L. c. 94I § 1, M.G.L. c. 94G § 1, 935 CMR §§ 500.002, §§ 501.002, §§ 
500.181(4)(a), and §§ 501.181(4)(a) are incorporated herein by reference.  
Sec. 28-7. Transparency of Local Approval Process:
(1) Data shall be published regarding the number and composition of applicants, identifying each pre-
verified or verified social equity business, social equity program participant, or economic empowerment
priority applicant.
(2) The following information shall be published in a conspicuous location at City offices and on the City 
website:
(a) All required steps of the local approval process including, but not limited to, all associated fees,
deadlines, and meeting schedules for local bodies involved in the local approval process;
(b) Identification of key individuals involved in the local approval process, including, but not 
limited to, their name, title, business address, and business contact information such as email 
address or phone number; 
(c) A list of all documentation required by the local approval process, in downloadable form and 
paper form; 
(d) Identification of application criteria for local approval to operate a marijuana establishment or 
medical marijuana treatment center, and scoring methodologies relied on by the City;
City Council                                         November 10, 2026                                                  Page 16 of 22
(e) General and individual scoring information for all license applicants;
(f) An explanation, in narrative form, of its reasoning for the approval or denial of an application; 
and
(g) Any other information required by the Commission as outlined in 935 CMR §§ 500.000 and §§ 
501.000.
Sec. 28-8. Practices for Host Community Agreement Negotiations
Host community agreement negotiations with individuals or entities pre-verified or verified as social equity 
businesses, and license applicants that have been designated as social equity program participants or economic 
empowerment priority applicants shall include but not be limited to, the following: 
(1) A standard evaluation form, or use a form developed by the Cannabis Control Commission, that scores 
components of an application. The evaluation form shall include consideration of equity in the overall 
evaluation score which must comprise not less than 25% of the total evaluation score. 
(2) This equity component shall include:
a. whether an individual, entity, or license applicant is pre-verified or verified by the Cannabis 
Control Commission as a social equity business; 
b. whether the license applicant is a social equity program participant;
c. whether the license applicant is an economic empowerment priority applicant;
d. whether a license applicant or pre-verified individual or entity has a prior marijuana-related 
criminal offense or conviction;
e. whether a license applicant or pre-verified individual or entity is part of an area of 
disproportionate Impact, as identified by the Cannabis Control Commission; or whether a pre-
verified individual is of Black, African American, Hispanic, Latino, Native American or 
indigenous descent, or a majority of a pre-verified entity or license applicant entity is 
comprised of individuals that are of Black, African American, Hispanic, Latino, Native 
American or indigenous descent.
(3) If additional marijuana establishments or medical marijuana treatment centers are allowed, at least 50% 
of those licenses, but no less than one license, above the previously established cap shall be reserved for
license applicants that are pre-verified or verified social equity businesses, social equity program 
participants, economic empowerment priority applicants, or all.
Sec. 28-9. Equity Standards for Host Community Agreements
(1) Negotiations of host community agreements with equity parties shall be prioritized. For the purposes of 
negotiations of a host community agreement for an application for licensure, equity parties are as 
follows:
a. A license applicant that is pre-verified or verified as a social equity business; or
b. A license applicant that has been designated as social equity program participants, economic 
empowerment priority applicants, or both. 
(2) Fees may be waived or reduced for an equity party to a host community agreement negotiation, 
including, but not limited to community impact fees, zoning, and occupancy fees.
(3) During host community agreement negotiations with an equity party the following shall occur:
a. Engage in an ongoing dialogue by providing multiple opportunities for discussion and 
negotiation of host community agreement terms including, at minimum, two conferences with 
an equity party; 
b. Include any attorney, authorized representative, or other advocate, if elected by an equity party, 
in all negotiation discussions and conferences; 
c. Promote language access by providing a certified interpreter or translator to assist an equity 
party who is a non-English speaker during all negotiation discussions and conferences;
d. Provide reasonable opportunities for an equity party to review a proposed host community 
agreement, term, or condition, outside of a negotiation conference, or to seek review or input by
a third party of their choice;
City Council                                         November 10, 2026                                                  Page 17 of 22
e. Negotiate the terms of a host community agreement in good faith, including consideration of 
flexible terms that may mitigate particular challenges affecting an equity party, such as access 
to capital, with all terms and clauses conspicuously identified and openly discussed; and  
f. Allow an equity party to propose an amendment to, or seek cancellation of, a host community 
agreement within thirty days from the date of execution of the host community agreement. 
(4) The negotiations may also:
a. Expedite or prioritize the local approval process for social equity businesses, social equity 
program participants, and economic empowerment priority applicants;  
b. Provide technical assistance for social equity businesses, social equity program participants, 
and economic empowerment priority applicants navigating the local approval process;  
c. Designate a municipal contact who shall work closely with social equity businesses, social 
equity program participants, and economic empowerment priority applicants in the local 
approval process from initial inquiry through the end of the permitting process; or  
d. Adopt an exclusivity period to permit social equity businesses for three years or until the goals 
of the exclusivity period have been met as determined by the municipality. 
(5) Negotiations shall not:
a. Use or employ undue influence, duress, coercion, intimidation, threats, or any strong-arm 
tactics;
b. Threaten loss of an equity party's position in its local application queue or delay to the 
processing of an equity party's application;
c. Compel an equity party to sign a host community agreement in any manner that conflicts with 
the practices required through applicable state law and regulations; and 
d. Negotiate or discontinue negotiations with an equity party in bad faith.
Sec. 28-10. Municipal Equity Plan
(1) An equity plan shall be developed to promote and encourage full participation in the regulated cannabis 
industry by individuals from communities disproportionately harmed by cannabis prohibition and 
enforcement. 
(2) The equity plan shall be publicized at City Hall and on the City’s website.
(3) The equity plan shall
a. Encourage applications from business and individuals that would meet the definition of social 
equity businesses, social equity program participants, and Economic empowerment priority 
applicants as determined by the Commission; and 
b. Include goals, programs, and measurements the City will utilize to promote and encourage 
equity participation.
Sec. 28-11. Notification
Notification of this this ordinance and any other information shall be provided to the Cannabis Control 
Commission as required by applicable state law and regulations in a timely manner.
Sec. 28-12. Implementation
This ordinance shall not be implemented in a manner that conflicts or interferes with the M.G.L. c. 94G or c. 
94I, or with the regulations promulgated thereunder, including 935 CMR §§ 500.000 or §§ 501.000.
Sec. 28-13. Severability
If any provisions of this ordinance shall be held to be invalid, those provisions shall be severable, and the
remaining sections shall be valid with full force and effect.

COUNCIL VOTE:
1. Letter from the City Council to the Joint Committee on Education re: Support for Senate Bill S.457 – An
Act to Establish the Middle School Innovation Fund
Summary of Discussion: Councilor Memhard stated that he had brought the matter forward after attending a
tour of the O’Maley Innovation School and their science lab and facilities. 
Councilor Memhard read the following letter into the record:
“Dear Chairs and Members of the Joint Committee on Education:
On behalf of the City of Gloucester, the Gloucester City Council writes to express our enthusiastic support for
Senate Bill S.457, An Act to Establish the Middle School Innovation Fund, introduced by Senate Minority Leader
Bruce Tarr.
In Gloucester, we have witnessed firsthand the transformative impact of hands-on, project-centered STEM
education. The success of the Science Center at O'Maley Innovation Middle School stands as a model of how
experiential, group-based learning can ignite student curiosity, build critical problem-solving skills, and prepare
young minds for future academic and career pathways. S.457 provides an essential framework to replicate these
opportunities across public school districts statewide.
Middle school represents a pivotal crossroads in student development. Engaging students early in collaborative
science, technology, engineering, and math initiatives ensures they remain inspired and equipped for high school
and post-secondary opportunities. By establishing a dedicated grant program, S.457 will empower local school
districts to implement innovative curricula, acquire necessary learning tools, and foster vibrant educational
environments tailored to middle school students.
The Gloucester City Council strongly urges the Joint Committee on Education to report S.457 favorably out of
committee. Investing in middle school innovation is an investment in the workforce, leadership, and prosperity
of the Commonwealth.
Thank you for your consideration of this critical legislation and for your continued commitment to public
education in Massachusetts.”
Councilor Page asked how many innovation middle schools there were in the State. Councilor Memhard stated
that he did not have that information. 
MOTION: On a motion by Councilor Memhard, seconded by Councilor Page, the City Council voted 8 in
favor, 0 opposed, 1 absent, to send a letter in support for Senate Bill S.457-An Act to Establish the Middle
School Innovation Fund.
